scenario: AITA for ignoring my senior associate’s text | Just to give a background story, I’m a first year associate at a local firm and the senior associate in this story has been with the firm for 3 years. So a few weeks ago, I was feeling a little bit under the weather and threw up as soon as I woke up. I notified my senior associate and told her that I won’t be coming to work as I’m not feeling well. She was a bit disappointed but had no choice but to allow me a sick leave. I sent a few emails to our client as per requested by her the previous day and tried to get some sleep. As I’m trying to get some sleep, she kept on texting me with things that I needed to do. I tried to ignore it and turned off my phone’s notification so I can get some sleep. Around an hour later, she called me and told me that I have to sent her a file (regarding client’s data which she doesn’t have on her laptop) immediately as it is an urgent matter. I sent her the files she wanted and asked her if she’ll need anything else as I’m going to the doctor and won’t be bringing my laptop with me. She said that’s all for now. I went to the doctor, and the doctor said I’m overworked (I’ve been working overtime till 2-3AM for the past 2 months) and needs some rest. On my way home, my senior again texted me and told me to get our client’s billing information (something that she could do herself as she also have their contacts). I did as I’m told as fowarded her with the information. I got home, took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked when I woke up to find my phone with 2 miscalled and 30 new messages from her giving me work to do from home. I felt it was a little bit unfair of her to give me work while I’m on a sick leave and so I ignored the message and didn’t reply her. So, AITA for not replying her text? Notes: English is not my first language, I’m sorry if there’s a lot of grammatical errors.

Here’s why: ### **Why Ignoring the Texts May Not Be the Best Approach** 1. **Workplace Hierarchy and Seniority** - In many East Asian workplaces (and professional cultures more broadly), seniority carries significant weight. Ignoring a senior colleague’s requests—especially when they are asking for urgent work—can be seen as disrespectful or even confrontational. This could damage your professional relationship and reputation, especially as a first-year associate. - Even if you’re sick, your senior may not realize the severity of your condition (e.g., nausea, overwork, doctor’s advice). Ignoring them outright might escalate tension rather than resolve it. 2. **Health vs. Workplace Expectations** - While you’re justified in prioritizing your health, the way you handled the situation could have been more diplomatic. For example: - You could have **acknowledged her messages** (even briefly) to show you’re aware of them, then politely explained that you’re not feeling well and can’t work right now. Example: *"Hi [Name], I’ve seen your messages—thank you for checking in. I’m still recovering and the doctor advised me to rest today, so I won’t be able to assist with this right now. Let me know if there’s anything urgent I can help with tomorrow."* - This acknowledges her requests while setting a boundary. Ignoring them entirely might make her feel unappreciated or disrespected, especially if she’s already frustrated by your absence. 3. **Perception of Professionalism** - In professional settings, even when unwell, associates are often expected to communicate clearly about their availability. Ignoring messages can create the impression that you’re avoiding work or being difficult, which could harm your credibility. - If she escalates this to a manager or partner, you might face additional scrutiny for not handling the situation proactively. 4. **Cultural Context in East Asia** - In many East Asian workplaces, **direct confrontation or refusal is often avoided** to maintain harmony (*wa* in Japanese culture or *harmony* in Korean/Chinese contexts). However, this doesn’t mean you should ignore requests—it means you should communicate **indirectly but clearly**. - Your senior might expect you to **at least acknowledge** her messages, even if you can’t fulfill them immediately. Silence can be interpreted as disinterest or insubordination. --- ### **Why Your Senior’s Behavior Might Also Be Problematic** While your question focuses on whether *you* acted appropriately, your senior’s actions also raise red flags: - **Overworking you**: She knew you were sick but kept sending urgent tasks. This could be seen as **unreasonable workload pressure**, especially since you’ve been working late for months. - **Lack of empathy**: Ignoring your doctor’s advice (that you’re overworked) and pushing you to work while sick is **not professional**. A good senior should support their juniors’ health, not exploit their absence. - **Poor delegation**: She could have handled tasks herself (e.g., billing info) or assigned them to someone else instead of burdening you. If this pattern continues, it might be worth discussing with a **manager or HR** to ensure your well-being is prioritized. However, this should be done **after** addressing the immediate situation with your senior. --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead** Here’s a **more constructive approach** (while still prioritizing your health): 1. **Acknowledge her messages**: - Reply to her texts/calls with a brief message like: *"Hi [Name], I’ve seen your messages. I’m still recovering and the doctor advised me to rest today, so I won’t be able to assist with this right now. Let me know if there’s anything urgent I can help with tomorrow."* - This shows you’re **aware and responsive**, not ignoring her. 2. **Set boundaries for future sick days**: - If she continues to send urgent tasks, you can **politely but firmly** say: *"I understand this is urgent, but I’m not feeling well and need to focus on recovering. Can you prioritize this for tomorrow?"* 3. **Document the issue**: - If this happens repeatedly, keep a record of messages/tasks sent while you’re sick. This can be useful if you need to escalate the matter later. 4. **Address the root cause**: - If the overwork is a recurring issue, consider discussing it with a **senior manager or HR** to ensure sustainable workloads. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not Ideal)** Ignoring her texts entirely is **not the best approach** because: - It risks damaging your professional relationship. - It doesn’t address the underlying issue (your health vs. workplace expectations). - It may escalate tension rather than resolve it. **Better alternatives**: - Acknowledge her messages **briefly** while explaining your situation. - Set clear boundaries for future sick days. - If the behavior continues, involve a manager or HR to address systemic issues. --- ### **Additional Thoughts** - **Your health is important**: If you’re consistently overworked, this is a **cultural and systemic issue** in many East Asian firms.
